title: Four C/C++ libraries ported to pure managed .NET on a $20 plan
text:
I'm between jobs right now, and I'm bad at sitting idle. I could have built yet another portfolio site with a chatbot and a smiling robot avatar, but I wanted to spend the time on something people might actually use.

There was a second reason. My feed is full of stories about LLM agents that burn thousands of dollars in tokens overnight. I suspected that most of them say more about the process than about the tools, and I wanted to check that on real work.

So over about three weeks, with Claude Code on a $20/month Pro plan as the main tool (plus $100 of promotional credits that were expiring anyway, and some free-tier model sessions for the routine parts), I ported four native libraries to fully managed C#, with no P/Invoke and no native binaries:

- Leptonica.Managed - Leptonica 1.87.0, image processing and the base of Tesseract OCR; about 2,700 functions. https://github.com/sensboston/Leptonica.Managed - Stb.Managed - seven of Sean Barrett's stb libraries (image load/save, resize, TrueType, rect_pack, DXT, Perlin). https://github.com/sensboston/Stb.Managed - MetadataSharp - EXIF/MakerNotes, IPTC, XMP and ICC read/write. Not a port: written from the specs, with Exiv2 as the reference. https://github.com/sensboston/MetadataSharp - MdfLibrary.Managed - mdflib, the ASAM MDF format of automotive data loggers, with the same API as its Windows-only C++/CLI wrapper, plus a cross-platform viewer with live CAN capture. https://github.com/sensboston/mdflib.net

All four are on NuGet under MIT.

I wouldn't call this vibe coding. The model wrote most of the code, but the work went the way any port of this size should go, with or without an LLM. First we discussed the architecture: what maps to what in C#, what stays bit-exact and what may be optimized, what is ported and what is left out. Then came a written plan in stages, each with a measurable exit condition. Before the first line of the port, the native library was built and became the oracle; the tests compare against it, not against the model's opinion of what the output should be. Then the work went in small batches, each merged only when CI was green.

The checks are boring on purpose: pixel by pixel against Leptonica's golden files, byte by byte against stb, tag by tag against exiv2 on its own test corpus, file by file against the native MdfLibrary. Parsers are fuzzed. It still isn't bulletproof: the GPU path of Stb.Managed passed every test on ILGPU's CPU accelerator and did not work at all on a real CUDA card. Tests are only as honest as the hardware they run on.

One result surprised me: the managed code is faster than C on most operations - about 1.3-2.0x single-threaded for Leptonica (regular Release build of the C library) and 1.5-1.8x for stb (-O3 -march=native). The JIT emits Vector128/256/512 code for the actual CPU, and Leptonica's C code has almost no SIMD. It is not faster everywhere: stb's hand-written SIMD resize still wins on one core, and JPEG on ARM64 is slower. The slow cases are listed in each repo.

Total extra cost beyond the subscription: $0. The expensive part was waiting for usage limits to reset; my patience turned out to be the scarcest resource in the project.

Happy to answer questions about the process, the verification, or the parts that went wrong.
author: sensboston

title: Show HN: Cerulion – Harness for Robotics, Gemini 3.8 Flash Matches GPT-6 Astra
text:
Hey HN! I'm Lakshay, and at Cerulion we cooked up a harness for physical AI. Built on top of our deterministic runtime, we now have MCP tools that let any LLM see and move a robot. It closes the loop with measurements so a model doesn't try to guess its way through the task, and imbues common sense and robotics best practices into the workflow.

We ran the numbers on LIBERO-PRO and quite frankly are a bit shocked. Gemini 3.8 Flash with Cerulion solved 73 of 100 LIBERO-PRO tasks. GPT-6 Astra on a bare 3-tool baseline (arXiv:2610.30051) solved 71, at about 12x the cost and 3x the wall time per run. Flash on that same baseline solved 25.

Guys. Gemini 3.8 Flash matched GPT-6 Astra for robotics. Model intelligence is not the bottleneck. A harness is all you need ;)

Star us and follow along. Try the quickstart, lmk what you guys wanna see next. I'll post again soon! (teaser: my Nespresso machine is getting a lot of attention from my robot arm)
author: lakshays

title: Re: GPT-6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design ...
text:
I did my PhD at the Baker lab, haven't had the time to properly read this over but some initial thoughts:

Makes total sense that they'd be working on this, it's something we discussed in the lab as well as the likely future of this work - true integration of the language modeling capabilities with proteins, natively multimodal like it's done with images. Five years ago we laughed at people with galaxy brained ideas to train / fuse a protein and natural language model, advertising this idea of "give me a natural language request and the model spits out the sequence that does the thing". There are many objections - the annotated data is not there, trying to pose everything as a language modeling objective sounded really naive at the time, and there are lots of tasks that are structural/chemical in nature that require inference based on physical and chemical principles, which interpolating machine learning models shouldn't be able to do. Most of these objections still exist, but now we aren't laughing. I do think eventually these models will get there.

That said, this work of course advertises far more than it accomplishes/has some things that have me holding judgement. One is I don't see how they did train-test splitting, or if they attempted this at all. This is really important - for some of these tasks, they are comparing against "specialized models" that did pretty rigorous holdout evaluation.

Also binder design is basically the easiest task, super solved a million times in the past few years, and their designs just made helical bundles, I don't think this is particularly impressive in terms of pushing the frontier. There is a hierarchy of difficult problems in protein design and this is just really easy, especially because experimentally these helical bundles bind really well and make strong interfaces.

The antibody CDR design tasks are also probably fairly trivial? I'm not sure, I'm not deep into antibody dev/design but there are lots of structures and sequences of anti-pdl-1 antibodies, so again a case of train-test split. I'd be curious to see sequence homology to these published antibodies.

But yeah, my take is that at the object level, this work is not super impressive. At one level of remove, the fact that they are getting an LLM to do these tasks that are normally done by specialized protein language or structure models is impressive. And then at one more level of remove, it's a big gauntlet thrown, proof that they are pursuing this line of research. I wouldn't be surprised if it works much better, soon, with the pace of these things. And we know Anthropic is working on this as well - https://xinmingtu.cn/blog/2026/claude-opus-5-5-protein-seque....

Might have to find a new line of work soon lol, thought I had at least another 5 years left.

title: Launch HN: Versine (YC F26) – MCP to send and receive money
text:
Hey HN, we’re Harshith, Param, and Vishnu and we're building Versine (https://versine.com). Versine lets you send and request money just by talking or texting with your AI (think Venmo with an MCP). We’re software engineers who have worked on distributed systems at Stripe, Databricks, and Amazon.

Versine is an MCP that sits in front of a wallet with a balance. With it, your agent can do things like:

- Send money to someone with your approval (via passkey in our app)

- Send and request money to/from up to 100 people at once

- Send money to people without a Versine account (they cash out to their bank in 2 mins)

- Pay people without your explicit approval to trusted contacts (you can set this)

Here’s a demo: https://youtube.com/shorts/Q9X7zioEqi0

We started working on this because assistants are frustratingly hands-off when it comes to finance and money movement. You can have your assistant go through a receipt and map out all the amounts owed taking care of splitting the subtotal, taxes, tips, but at the end of it the assistant hands back work to you when you have to go out and make the Venmo transfer.

Our current solution is oriented towards power users: those who want to automate everything through their agent use us to split dinners, group trips, or settle poker ledgers. We see ourselves unlocking more value for the general consumer as

1. More people turn into power users of agents, and 2. We expand to a more complete banking solution: deposits, transfers, wires, everything you can (and more) do with your bank offered as an MCP.

Behind the scenes, each user has a self-custodial stablecoin wallet storing USDC on Base. With self-custodial wallets, users own their keys, meaning money can’t be sent without their approval.

Interestingly, we were almost forced into this solution because we had around 4 weeks to build this product (after a pivot), and traditional fiat with a partner bank would have caused far too many regulatory and compliance slowdowns.

Because of that, the only fast option that remained was using stablecoin wallets. It also ensures we aren't a Money Services Business (MSB) since we don’t hold control or access to the user’s funds.

Each call to the wallet creates what we call one-time or recurring standing permissions. For a one-time payment, your agent makes an MCP call, and you receive a notification in our mobile app. Once you swipe up in the app and approve with a passkey (or your device’s biometric method), we create a one-time permission that instructs your wallet to send $X to your recipient’s address.

Trusted contacts let your agent send money to people that you’ve previously authorized without explicit passkey approval. Generally, these are people that you’d trust to send your money back even if your agent made a mistake.

We’re also able to support sending money to someone off Versine using claim forwarding, where the user authorizes us to forward a specific amount to a future address (which we create once we verify a recipient's OTP).

Param worked on scaling vector search at Databricks and harness evals at Glean. Harshith worked on core Stripe Connect fee-processing infrastructure and built an AWS Fargate autoscaler at Amazon. Vishnu worked on intent-based agent testing infrastructure at Amazon. None of us were experienced in stablecoin or crypto infra before working on Versine but our distributed systems experience has helped us a lot.

We'd love for you guys to try it! It's available on iOS and Android and as an MCP on ChatGPT and Claude. We also support a public MCP and REST API for other agents.

Please let us know how you find it and if it works as you'd hoped!

https://versine.com

title: Re: Claude Desktop or Terminal?...
text:
I run the terminal app in tmux on a remote machine so Claude can keep working when I pack up my laptop. I often enable remote control and manage it with the desktop or phone app, but the session has to be initiated and connected to /rc and terminal is the easiest way to do that.

Also, I may have three sessions on three different billing accounts going on different machines, and again that’s just easier to manage as terminal programs. I can have two terminals side-by-side and be prompting one while the other makes progress, whereas the desktop app can only look at one at a time and its account-switching is very clumsy.

The only upsides to the desktop app IMO are related to cut/paste… I can paste images directly into it, and when I copy text out it never includes excess newlines or other wrapping artifacts.
author: sayotte

title: Re: Show HN: Keeping faces and features consistent acr...
text:
I created joonoo.art to turn family photos into picture books and comics. I was inspired to do it last summer because my granddaughter was very enthusiastic when I made up stories with her as the hero.

It's been a major struggle to get it working consistently, though. It's hard enough to have ONE character be consistent in a series of images you create using image generation models like nano banana, but to maintain consistency of up to 4 main characters, all the side characters, the props (like dragons, submarines, spaceships, or what have you) throughout the book is a Herculean struggle! On top of that, I got really ambitious and wanted to do a worldwide launch supporting 24 languages - you can imagine the amount of testing it takes! It really buried me - especially as a side project.

I nearly gave up on it. After I launched last year, I got a few orders and the customers who got the books (primarily in English in the U.S.) were happy, but I did not feel comfortable publicizing the product, so it languished. But then Fable came along and gave me hope. After a few months working with the great capabilities of Fable and Claude Code, I was able to relaunch - this time in fewer languages and countries.

As the public starts to use it, they are stretching the limits of what's possible, so it's a constant struggle, but it's also a great learning and hardening experience! To others struggling with similar quests, I would strongly recommend the superpowers framework for Claude Code - and building in the testing is the most important thing you could do to succeed. I would also love to hear if you have any advice for me.

The website itself was created using the impeccable plugin and Google fonts - and design and consumer-friendliness was paramount. I am very pleased with it, and customers have said that they love it. There are tons of examples - mostly AI-generated family photos and the comics and picture books created using those photos.

For example, https://joonoo.art/books/mystery-of-the-lighthouse-key/read shows you a photo of 3 siblings and the full comic book that was created using that photo.

You can find tons more example books and comics to scroll through in video form here: https://joonoo.art/videos. If you'd rather scroll through the pages, start here: https://joonoo.art/comics or here: https://joonoo.art/picture-books

I am very eager to hear from you!

title: Re: Anthropic Staff Openly Talk About ‘Taking Over the...
text: I think I can speak with confidence that Anthropic is not going to take over the world or a nation.  That would require more developed robotics capability than exists, and it would require a company that is much more connected to fabrication and physical supply chains.  They don't even own their own data centers and their stock valuation is already plummeting.  Anthropic models could ransom, disrupt and possibly even destroy the world economic system, but physical takeover is not coming from this company.  I would watch someone like Musk more carefully after a decade or so of robotics development.
